---
title: "Question 2 Analysis"
---

# Question of Interest
Is there a relation between the classes people have taken and their preference for certain areas of data science?

# Analysis Plan

1. **Variables, files, respondents**
    - IV: classes taken (grouped into subject categories plus a pre-req category)
    - DV: areas of data science selected as interesting (image analysis, neural networks, time series, data engineering, text analysis, software integration, data visualization, predictive modeling, statistical modeling, databases, algorithms)
    - Files: `background-clean.csv` (classes), `interest-clean.csv` (areas); `cleaned_combined_data.csv` has both joined by `response_id`
    - Respondents: all 49 who answered both surveys
2. **Data preparation**
    - Every selection becomes a binary (TRUE = selected, FALSE = not selected) since multiple classes/areas can be chosen
    - Group individual classes into subject categories. A respondent is "in" a category if they took at least one class in it
    - "Other" write-ins for areas are not handled for now (too few and too varied to categorize)
3. **Summaries, plots, models**
    - Frequency table of category x area counts (what is the raw overlap?)
    - Proportion table: of those who took a category, what share chose each area?
    - Heatmap of the difference in proportions (took category vs. did not take category), same approach as Question 1
    - Fisher's exact test per category/area pair (tells us whether a difference could plausibly be noise)
4. **Key choices to check**
    - How classes are grouped into categories (check the grouping isn't driving the result)
    - Categories with very unbalanced groups (almost everyone or almost no one took them) are interpreted cautiously
    - Multiple testing: 11 areas x N categories means many tests, so p-values are adjusted (Benjamini-Hochberg)
5. **One limitation**
    - Small sample (49), and one person appears in many cells, so tests are not independent. Results are exploratory, not confirmatory.

**Why not a plain chi-square test?** Respondents can fall into several categories/areas at once, so a single contingency table would count the same person many times and break the independence assumption. Instead, each category/area pair gets its own 2x2 table (one person, one cell), and Fisher's exact test is used because expected counts are often below 5.

```{r Load in Packages and Data}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

data <- read_csv("data/cleaned_combined_data.csv")
```

```{r Identify Course and Area Columns}
area_cols <- data %>% select(image_analysis:algorithms) %>% colnames()
area_cols
```

```{r Group Classes into Categories}
# The combined data already has a count column per category (from the Question 1 script).
# prereq_core is left out: everyone took at least one of those classes, so there's no comparison group.
category_cols <- c("intro_ds", "programming", "adv_stat_ml", "time_series_stoch", "other_dept")

# "Took the category" = at least one class in it
data_grouped <- data %>% mutate(across(all_of(category_cols), ~ .x > 0))

# Check: every category should have both takers and non-takers
data_grouped %>% summarise(across(all_of(category_cols), list(took = ~ sum(.x), not = ~ sum(!.x))))
```

```{r Aggregating Results}
# Proportion of respondents who took each category
categories_taken <- data_grouped %>% select(all_of(category_cols)) %>% colSums() %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column()
colnames(categories_taken) <- c("category", "count")
categories_taken <- categories_taken %>% mutate(prop = count / nrow(data_grouped))
categories_taken

# Same for areas
areas_of_interest <- data_grouped %>% select(all_of(area_cols)) %>% colSums() %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column()
colnames(areas_of_interest) <- c("area", "count")
areas_of_interest <- areas_of_interest %>% mutate(prop = count / nrow(data_grouped))
areas_of_interest %>% arrange(desc(prop))
```

```{r Creating a 2 way frequency table}
# Counts of respondents choosing each category/area pair.
# Margins will exceed 49 since one person can be in multiple categories and select multiple areas.
category_area_count_table <- matrix(nrow = length(category_cols), ncol = length(area_cols))
colnames(category_area_count_table) <- area_cols
rownames(category_area_count_table) <- category_cols

for(cat in category_cols){
  counts <- data_grouped %>% filter(.data[[cat]] == TRUE) %>% select(all_of(area_cols)) %>% colSums()
  category_area_count_table[match(cat, category_cols),] <- counts
}
category_area_count_table %>% as.data.frame()
```

```{r Proportion Differences}
# For each category: proportion choosing an area among those who took it, minus the proportion among those who did not.
# Positive = people who took the category are more interested in that area.
pair_results <- expand_grid(category = category_cols, area = area_cols) %>%
  mutate(
    n_took = map_int(category, ~ sum(data_grouped[[.x]])),
    n_not = nrow(data_grouped) - n_took,
    prop_took = map2_dbl(category, area, ~ mean(data_grouped[[.y]][data_grouped[[.x]]])),
    prop_not = map2_dbl(category, area, ~ mean(data_grouped[[.y]][!data_grouped[[.x]]])),
    prop_diff = prop_took - prop_not,
    # Fisher's exact test on the 2x2 table (took category x selected area)
    p_value = map2_dbl(category, area, ~ fisher.test(table(factor(data_grouped[[.x]], levels = c(FALSE, TRUE)),
                                                           factor(data_grouped[[.y]], levels = c(FALSE, TRUE))))$p.value)
  ) %>%
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"))

# Pairs with biggest differences. 
pair_results %>% arrange(desc(abs(prop_diff))) %>% head(10)
```

```{r Main Plot}
pair_results$category <- factor(pair_results$category, levels = categories_taken %>% arrange(count) %>% pull(category))
pair_results$area <- factor(pair_results$area, levels = areas_of_interest %>% arrange(count) %>% pull(area))

prop_diff_plot_q2 <- ggplot(pair_results, aes(x = category, y = area, fill = prop_diff)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(prop_diff, 2)), col = "white") +
  labs(x = "Class Category Taken", y = "Area of Data Science",
       title = "Difference in Area Interest: Took Category vs. Did Not Take",
       subtitle = "Positive = more interest among those who took the category") +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 9))

prop_diff_plot_q2
```

```{r Significance Table}
# Pairs with a raw p < 0.05, with BH-adjusted p alongside. Expect few to survive adjustment with n = 49.
significant_pairs <- pair_results %>%
  filter(p_value < 0.05) %>%
  arrange(p_value) %>%
  transmute(Category = category, Area = area, `Took Prop.` = round(prop_took, 2), `Not Took Prop.` = round(prop_not, 2),
            Difference = round(prop_diff, 2), `p (raw)` = round(p_value, 3), `p (BH adj.)` = round(p_adj, 3))
significant_pairs
```

# Methodology
Within each class category, respondents are split into two groups: those who took at least one class in the category and those who did not. In each group I calculate the proportion who also expressed interest in a specific area of data science. Each heatmap cell is the difference between those two proportions.

For example: a value of 0.30 for `programming` and `neural_networks` would mean the proportion interested in neural networks is 30 percentage points higher among people who took a programming class than among those who did not.

I am wary of conclusions for categories where nearly everyone (or nearly no one) took a class, since the smaller group's proportions swing a lot with a single response.

# Extra Ideas:
- Logistic regression per area (area selected ~ categories taken) to see the effect of each category while holding the others fixed, since categories overlap.
- Count the number of classes taken as a single "preparation" score and compare it to the number of areas selected.

```{r}
save(pair_results, significant_pairs, prop_diff_plot_q2, category_area_count_table, file = "question_2_results.rda")
```
